## TL;DR

This change addresses both original lifecycle failures and the follow-up request to make Board and Pipeline cards agree. A single resolver in the UI library now derives active-task status, stuck state, and available action from handoff, check, engineer, pause, queue, and quiet-time signals. Both TaskCard and PipelineCard use it. A running handoff/check wins through verify, review, and capture; stale telemetry cannot turn that work into PAUSED or Stuck. Separately, a deferred handoff with queued messages resumes an idle engineer through the existing message-delivery path, records why it resumed, and stops after the bounded retry count.

## Work and rationale

The original card bug came from treating the engineer process as the practical definition of active work. Server finalization can continue after that process exits, so process presence alone is insufficient. The shared `resolveSharedTaskCardStatus` function now checks handoff status, check execution, and remote validation before queue, input, engineer, and idle states. It produces the status label, stuck classification, and action together. TaskCard and PipelineCard therefore render the same result from the same signals instead of independently guessing whether a task is paused or stuck.

An explicitly paused active task remains distinguishable through the paused-task IDs returned by the running-agent endpoint and exposed by the repository store. That signal is cleared when the task resumes or its run/status changes. A task only becomes Stuck when no work is in flight, it is not explicitly paused, the existing quiet threshold has elapsed, and the current evidence indicates a stuck condition. Pipeline status chips now use the same resolver label for Stuck and needs-input states, including failed handoff checks, while in-flight status uses the shared running-check line. Actions follow that same result: active work has no pause/restart action, an engineer can be paused, and an idle/paused task can be restarted.

For the server-side deadlock, turn cleanup already notices that queued human messages block review. At that point, after the old turn is removed, the implementation records the deferred status and an activity reason (`↻ resuming engineer to read queued message`), increments a persisted attempt counter, and invokes the normal queued-message delivery route. That route retains responsibility for preparing and launching the next turn. It does not start another turn when one is already running, the task is paused, or the normal queue/handoff guards reject delivery. The counter is read from the current task file rather than a possibly stale in-memory object and is capped using the existing small retry bounds to prevent an automatic loop.

Regression coverage includes the four handoff phases, explicit pause and restart behavior, a deferred queued-message resume with Activity evidence and retry-cap behavior, and paired Board/Pipeline assertions using the same task state for verify, pause, and Stuck. Focused tests passed for the UI status, card actions, pause/resume endpoint, and queued-message delivery. The UI typecheck and production build also passed after the shared-status changes.

## Approaches tried

I first traced the existing TaskCard hint/action logic and the repository store’s server-backed handoff state. For the UI fix, I kept one resolver and passed its source signals into PipelineCard, rather than implementing a second Pipeline-specific status tree. PipelineCard calls the resolver itself, and TaskCard calls the same function, which makes labels and actions comparable and testable. The board’s check-progress component accepts the shared status line so it does not replace that label with a separate interpretation.

For deferred messages, I reused the existing message-delivery path instead of inventing a new runner start flow. This keeps session selection and queued-message preparation consistent with other resume behavior. I also moved retry-count reads to fresh persisted task content after identifying that a reused task object could otherwise undercount earlier resumes.

## Challenges and blockers

Earlier handoff attempts failed for several different reasons: one server gate timed out, a test gate failed with truncated output, and a later gate refused because the branch HEAD moved while the check was running. The latest review report (pass 1) found no code bugs and requested new screenshot evidence because its `/work` capture was missing and its available home-page shot was from an older tree. I have not claimed that evidence was refreshed; the managed handoff capture must confirm it against the current tree.

The first full scoped gate on this tree completed its build and ran all 358 changed-path test files, but identified three compatibility regressions in status precedence: PM activity obscured an engineer, stale-process status conflicted with the requested “never Stuck while an engineer runs” rule, and an underspecified needs-input task fell through to Paused. I changed the resolver order, retained the actionable needs-input flag, and updated the conflicting stale-process test to match the new requirement. The four affected UI suites passed (64 tests). I then rebuilt the UI and reran the required scoped gate on checkpoint `2333ca1d`: the remote suite passed all 358 changed-path test files (4,958 passed, 1 skipped), and formatting, lint, build, CSS/theme guards, rendered contrast, and UI smoke all passed locally. HEAD remained `2333ca1d` throughout that run.

The previous review requested a fresh card screenshot because the capture on its reviewed tree was missing/stale. I re-declared the default `/work` `card:checksProgress` shot with a task-card highlight for the new handoff capture. The capture itself is managed by RepoOS at handoff and is not yet observed in this session. No task status file was edited by hand; no source changes were made after the green check.

## Key learnings

An engineer process ending does not mean task work has ended: server finalization can still be verifying, reviewing, or capturing evidence. UI lifecycle labels and controls should therefore come from the server-backed work signals, with process state treated as one input among several. Board and Pipeline views can silently diverge if each composes those inputs on its own, so a shared pure resolver plus component-level equality tests is a practical guard.

Automatic recovery needs both an explicit activity reason and a durable bound. Persisted counters avoid stale-object mistakes, while the existing queued-message delivery guards prevent duplication when a turn is already underway. Finally, a handoff check must run against a stable branch head; a result from a moving tree cannot safely be attached to the committed handoff.
